category: Calculus II: Function Properties, Asymptotics, Series Tools, Integral Transforms & Vector Calculus
description: Symbolic function-property analysis (domain, range, continuity, monotonicity, convexity, periodicity, singularities, injectivity), asymptotic solvers and comparisons, limit superior/inferior, series manipulation (inverse and composed series, Pade approximants, convergence tests), additional integral transforms (bilateral Laplace, Mellin, Hankel, Hilbert, Radon, Fourier sine/cosine, Fourier coefficients and generating functions), implicit and difference derivatives, and vector calculus in curvilinear coordinates (line and surface integrals, coordinate charts, field transformation).

tools.name: FunctionDomain
tools.description: Finds the set of real (or complex) values of the variables for which a function is defined, returned as inequalities/conditions; FunctionRange finds the set of values the function takes. Both handle piecewise, algebraic and transcendental expressions and accept assumptions, and are the symbolic tools for validating formulas and setting plot ranges.
tools.usage:
FunctionDomain[f, x]
FunctionDomain[f, {x, y}]
FunctionDomain[f, x, Complexes]
FunctionRange[f, x, y]
FunctionRange[{f, cons}, x, y]
FunctionRange[f, {x1, x2}, y, Reals]

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Symbol used to express the range.

tools.example:
FunctionDomain[Log[x^2 - 1]/Sqrt[x + 3], x] (* -3 < x < -1 || x > 1 *)
FunctionRange[x/(1 + x^2), x, y] (* -1/2 <= y <= 1/2 *)
FunctionRange[{Sqrt[x], 0 < x < 4}, x, y]

tools.name: FunctionContinuous
tools.description: Symbolic regularity tests over a domain: FunctionContinuous (continuity), FunctionAnalytic (real-analytic / holomorphic), FunctionMeromorphic, plus FunctionDiscontinuities (set of discontinuity points), FunctionSingularities (points where the function or its analysis fails) and FunctionPoles (poles with orders). Use them before applying theorems, choosing integration methods or locating branch cuts.
tools.usage:
FunctionContinuous[f, x]
FunctionContinuous[{f, cons}, x]
FunctionAnalytic[f, x]
FunctionMeromorphic[f, z, Complexes]
FunctionDiscontinuities[f, x]
FunctionSingularities[f, x]
FunctionSingularities[f, x, Complexes]
FunctionPoles[f, z]
FunctionPoles[f, z, "Orders"]
tools.example:
FunctionContinuous[Tan[x], x] (* False *)
FunctionDiscontinuities[Tan[x], x] (* Mod[x - Pi/2, Pi] == 0 *)
FunctionPoles[1/(z^2 (z - 1)), z] (* {{0, 2}, {1, 1}} with orders *)
FunctionSingularities[Sqrt[x - 1] Log[x], x]

tools.name: FunctionMonotonicity
tools.description: Determines whether a function is increasing/decreasing (strictly or not) on a domain, FunctionConvexity whether it is convex/concave, FunctionSign its sign, and FunctionPeriod its period (for periodic functions), each returning a definite answer, a condition, or Indeterminate. These enable rigorous curve analysis, optimization preconditions (convexity) and choosing Fourier series periods automatically.
tools.usage:
FunctionMonotonicity[f, x]
FunctionMonotonicity[{f, cons}, x]
FunctionConvexity[f, x]
FunctionConvexity[{f, cons}, {x, y}]
FunctionSign[f, x]
FunctionSign[{f, cons}, x]
FunctionPeriod[f, x]
tools.example:
FunctionMonotonicity[{x^3 - 3 x, x > 1}, x] (* 1: increasing *)
FunctionConvexity[x^2 + y^2 - x y, {x, y}] (* 1: convex *)
FunctionSign[{Sin[x], 0 < x < Pi}, x] (* 1 *)
FunctionPeriod[Sin[3 x] + Cos[2 x], x] (* 2 Pi *)

tools.name: FunctionInjective
tools.description: Tests whether a function is injective (one-to-one), FunctionSurjective whether it maps onto a target set, and FunctionBijective both - over reals, complexes, integers or restricted domains; needed to justify inverse functions (InverseFunction) and change of variables in integrals and probability transformations.
tools.usage:
FunctionInjective[f, x]
FunctionInjective[{f, cons}, x]
FunctionSurjective[{f, cons}, x, y]
FunctionBijective[{f, cons}, x, y]
FunctionInjective[f, x, Integers]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Expression or list of expressions (vector function).

tools.example:
FunctionInjective[x^2, x] (* False *)
FunctionInjective[{x^2, x > 0}, x] (* True *)
FunctionBijective[{Exp[x], x > 0, y > 1}, x, y] (* True *)

tools.name: AsymptoticSolve
tools.description: Asymptotic solvers: AsymptoticSolve gives asymptotic expansions of roots of equations near a point or a known solution, AsymptoticDSolveValue of differential equations (regular/irregular singular points, WKB, perturbation series in a parameter), AsymptoticRSolveValue of recurrences, AsymptoticIntegrate of integrals (Laplace/stationary-phase type) and AsymptoticSum/AsymptoticProduct of sums and products; AsymptoticExpectation/AsymptoticProbability handle distributions. They deliver leading-order behaviour where exact solutions do not exist.
tools.usage:
AsymptoticSolve[eqn, {y, y0}, {x, x0, n}]
AsymptoticSolve[eqn, y, {x, x0, n}, Reals]
AsymptoticDSolveValue[ode, y[x], {x, x0, n}]
AsymptoticDSolveValue[ode, y[x], x -> Infinity]
AsymptoticDSolveValue[ode, y[x], x, {eps, 0, n}] (* perturbation in eps *)
AsymptoticRSolveValue[rec, a[n], n -> Infinity]
AsymptoticIntegrate[f, {x, a, b}, {lambda, Infinity, n}]
AsymptoticSum[f, {k, 1, n}, {n, Infinity, m}]

parameters.name: {lambda, Infinity, n}
parameters.description: Large parameter and number of terms.

tools.example:
AsymptoticSolve[y^3 + x y - 1 == 0, {y, 1}, {x, 0, 3}]
AsymptoticDSolveValue[x^2 y''[x] + x y'[x] + (x^2 - 1/4) y[x] == 0, y[x], x -> Infinity]
AsymptoticIntegrate[Exp[-lambda x^2] Cos[x], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}, {lambda, Infinity, 2}]
AsymptoticSum[1/k, {k, 1, n}, {n, Infinity, 3}] (* Log[n] + EulerGamma + 1/(2n) - ... *)

tools.name: AsymptoticEqual
tools.description: Asymptotic comparison relations between functions as x -> x0: AsymptoticEqual (same leading behaviour, f ~ c g), AsymptoticEquivalent (f/g -> 1), AsymptoticLess (o), AsymptoticLessEqual (O), AsymptoticGreater and AsymptoticGreaterEqual, with DiscreteAsymptotic for sequences; they formalize big-O reasoning and complexity comparisons symbolically. Asymptotic (listed) computes the expansions themselves.
tools.usage:
AsymptoticEqual[f, g, x -> x0]
AsymptoticEquivalent[f, g, x -> Infinity]
AsymptoticLess[f, g, x -> Infinity] (* f = o(g) *)
AsymptoticLessEqual[f, g, x -> Infinity] (* f = O(g) *)
AsymptoticGreater[f, g, x -> x0]
DiscreteAsymptotic[a[n], n -> Infinity]
tools.example:
AsymptoticLessEqual[n Log[n], n^2, n -> Infinity] (* True: n log n = O(n^2) *)
AsymptoticEquivalent[Sinh[x], Exp[x]/2, x -> Infinity] (* True *)
AsymptoticLess[Log[x], x^0.01, x -> Infinity] (* True *)

tools.name: MaxLimit
tools.description: MaxLimit and MinLimit give the limit superior and limit inferior of a function as x -> x0 (defined even when Limit does not exist, e.g. for oscillating functions), and DiscreteMaxLimit / DiscreteMinLimit the sequence versions; Limit itself takes Direction -> "FromAbove"/"FromBelow"/Reals/Complexes for one-sided and directional limits. Use them to characterize oscillatory or bounded non-convergent behaviour.
tools.usage:
MaxLimit[f, x -> x0]
MinLimit[f, x -> x0]
DiscreteMaxLimit[a[n], n -> Infinity]
DiscreteMinLimit[a[n], n -> Infinity]
Limit[f, x -> x0, Direction -> "FromAbove"]
Limit[f, x -> 0, Direction -> Complexes]
tools.example:
MaxLimit[Sin[1/x], x -> 0] (* 1 *)
MinLimit[Sin[1/x], x -> 0] (* -1 *)
DiscreteMaxLimit[(-1)^n (1 + 1/n), n -> Infinity] (* 1 *)
Limit[Abs[x]/x, x -> 0, Direction -> "FromBelow"] (* -1 *)

tools.name: InverseSeries
tools.description: Series manipulation: InverseSeries reverts a power series (series of the inverse function), ComposeSeries composes two series, SeriesData is the internal representation Series returns (Normal converts to a polynomial), and O[x]^n is the order symbol that truncates arithmetic on series automatically. These let you compute with truncated expansions exactly like generating functions.
tools.usage:
InverseSeries[Series[f, {x, 0, n}]]
InverseSeries[s, y]
ComposeSeries[s1, s2]
SeriesData[x, x0, {a0, a1, ...}, nmin, nmax, den]
Normal[series]
(1 + x + O[x]^4)^2
SeriesCoefficient[series, k]
tools.example:
s = Series[Sin[x], {x, 0, 7}];
InverseSeries[s, y] (* series of ArcSin *)
ComposeSeries[Series[Exp[x], {x, 0, 5}], Series[Sin[x], {x, 0, 5}]] (* Exp[Sin[x]] *)
(1 + x + x^2/2 + O[x]^3) (1 - x + O[x]^3) (* 1 + x^2/2 + O[x]^3 *)

tools.name: PadeApproximant
tools.description: Computes the Pade rational approximant of orders {m, n} to a function about a point, often converging far better than Taylor polynomials near poles; SumConvergence tests whether an infinite series converges (returning conditions on parameters) and Wronskian computes the Wronskian determinant of functions or of ODE solutions to test linear independence.
tools.usage:
PadeApproximant[f, {x, x0, {m, n}}]
PadeApproximant[f, {x, x0, n}] (* diagonal *)
SumConvergence[a[k], k]
SumConvergence[a[k], k, Method -> "RatioTest"]
Wronskian[{f1, f2, ...}, x]
Wronskian[ode, y, x]
tools.example:
PadeApproximant[Exp[x], {x, 0, {2, 2}}]
Plot[{Exp[x], PadeApproximant[Exp[x], {x, 0, {2, 2}}], Normal[Series[Exp[x], {x, 0, 4}]]}, {x, -4, 4}]
SumConvergence[1/k^p, k] (* p > 1 *)
Wronskian[{Sin[x], Cos[x]}, x] (* -1 *)

tools.name: ImplicitD
tools.description: Differentiates a function defined implicitly by an equation (or system) without solving it - dy/dx from F(x, y) = 0, higher and partial derivatives included - the symbolic form of implicit differentiation used for curves, constraint surfaces and sensitivity analysis; DifferenceQuotient gives (f(x+h) - f(x))/h and its multiple/partial versions for finite-difference derivations.
tools.usage:
ImplicitD[eqn, y, x]
ImplicitD[eqn, y, {x, n}]
ImplicitD[{eqn1, eqn2}, {y1, y2}, x]
ImplicitD[eqn, z, x, y] (* partial *)
DifferenceQuotient[f, {x, h}]
DifferenceQuotient[f, {x, n, h}]
tools.example:
ImplicitD[x^2 + y^2 == 1, y, x] (* -x/y *)
ImplicitD[x^3 + y^3 == 6 x y, y, {x, 2}]
DifferenceQuotient[x^2, {x, h}] (* 2 x + h *)

tools.name: BilateralLaplaceTransform
tools.description: Two-sided Laplace transform over the whole real line (with InverseBilateralLaplaceTransform) for signals defined for negative time, complementing the one-sided LaplaceTransform (listed); MellinTransform / InverseMellinTransform (scale-invariant transform used for asymptotics of integrals and number theory) and MellinConvolve are the multiplicative analogues. Regions of convergence are returned as conditions.
tools.usage:
BilateralLaplaceTransform[f, t, s]
InverseBilateralLaplaceTransform[F, s, t]
MellinTransform[f, x, s]
InverseMellinTransform[F, s, x]
MellinConvolve[f, g, x, y]
tools.example:
BilateralLaplaceTransform[Exp[-Abs[t]], t, s] (* 2/(1 - s^2), -1 < Re[s] < 1 *)
MellinTransform[Exp[-x], x, s] (* Gamma[s] *)
InverseMellinTransform[Gamma[s] Gamma[1 - s], s, x] (* 1/(1 + x) *)

tools.name: HankelTransform
tools.description: Hankel (Fourier-Bessel) transform of order nu with InverseHankelTransform, the radial Fourier transform for axisymmetric problems (optics, acoustics, cylindrical PDEs); HilbertTransform / InverseHilbertTransform give the analytic-signal transform used in envelope detection, and RadonTransform / InverseRadonTransform the symbolic Radon transform (image version: Radon). All work symbolically with conditions on parameters.
tools.usage:
HankelTransform[f, r, s]
HankelTransform[f, r, s, nu]
InverseHankelTransform[F, s, r]
HilbertTransform[f, t, u]
InverseHilbertTransform[F, u, t]
RadonTransform[f, {x, y}, {p, phi}]
InverseRadonTransform[F, {p, phi}, {x, y}]
tools.example:
HankelTransform[Exp[-r^2], r, s] (* Exp[-s^2/4]/2 *)
HilbertTransform[Cos[t], t, u] (* Sin[u] *)
RadonTransform[Exp[-x^2 - y^2], {x, y}, {p, phi}]

tools.name: FourierSinTransform
tools.description: Fourier sine and cosine transforms (and inverses) for functions on the half-line, natural for odd/even extensions and boundary-value problems; FourierCoefficient, FourierSinCoefficient and FourierCosCoefficient give the n-th Fourier series coefficients symbolically, and FourierTrigSeries / FourierSinSeries / FourierCosSeries build truncated trigonometric series (FourierSeries, listed, gives the complex-exponential form). FourierParameters selects the normalization convention throughout.
tools.usage:
FourierSinTransform[f, t, w]
FourierCosTransform[f, t, w]
InverseFourierSinTransform[F, w, t]
InverseFourierCosTransform[F, w, t]
FourierCoefficient[f, t, n]
FourierSinCoefficient[f, t, n]
FourierCosCoefficient[f, t, n]
FourierTrigSeries[f, t, n]
FourierTrigSeries[f, t, n, FourierParameters -> {a, b}]
tools.example:
FourierCosTransform[Exp[-t], t, w] (* Sqrt[2/Pi]/(1 + w^2) *)
FourierCoefficient[SquareWave[t/(2 Pi)], t, n]
FourierTrigSeries[Abs[t], t, 4] (* Pi/2 - 4 Cos[t]/Pi - 4 Cos[3 t]/(9 Pi) *)

tools.name: GeneratingFunction
tools.description: Computes the ordinary generating function Sum a[n] x^n of a sequence given by a formula, and ExponentialGeneratingFunction the exponential one (Sum a[n] x^n/n!); SeriesCoefficient and FindGeneratingFunction (listed) go the other way. Core tools of combinatorics and discrete probability (probability generating functions of count distributions).
tools.usage:
GeneratingFunction[a[n], n, x]
ExponentialGeneratingFunction[a[n], n, x]
GeneratingFunction[Fibonacci[n], n, x]
tools.example:
GeneratingFunction[Fibonacci[n], n, x] (* x/(1 - x - x^2) *)
ExponentialGeneratingFunction[BellB[n], n, x] (* Exp[Exp[x] - 1] *)
GeneratingFunction[Binomial[m, n], n, x] (* (1 + x)^m *)

tools.name: LineIntegrate
tools.description: Symbolic line integrals of scalar fields (with respect to arc length) or vector fields (work, circulation) along a curve given as a Line, Circle, parametric curve or region, and SurfaceIntegrate for surface integrals of scalar fields (area-weighted) or flux of vector fields through surfaces; NLineIntegrate / NSurfaceIntegrate are the numerical forms. They implement Green, Stokes and divergence-theorem computations directly in curvilinear or Cartesian coordinates.
tools.usage:
LineIntegrate[f, {x, y} \[Element] curve]
LineIntegrate[{Fx, Fy}, {x, y} \[Element] curve] (* vector: tangential component *)
LineIntegrate[f, {x, y, z} \[Element] Line[{p1, p2}]]
SurfaceIntegrate[f, {x, y, z} \[Element] surface]
SurfaceIntegrate[{Fx, Fy, Fz}, {x, y, z} \[Element] Sphere[]] (* flux *)
NLineIntegrate[f, {x, y} \[Element] curve]
NSurfaceIntegrate[F, {x, y, z} \[Element] surface]

parameters.name: curve / surface
parameters.description: Region: Line, Circle, Polygon, ParametricRegion, Sphere, Cylinder, ImplicitRegion, mesh...

tools.example:
LineIntegrate[{-y, x}, {x, y} \[Element] Circle[{0, 0}, 2]] (* 8 Pi: circulation *)
SurfaceIntegrate[{x, y, z}, {x, y, z} \[Element] Sphere[{0, 0, 0}, R]] (* 4 Pi R^3: flux, divergence theorem *)
NLineIntegrate[Sin[x y], {x, y} \[Element] ParametricRegion[{{Cos[t], Sin[2 t]}}, {{t, 0, Pi}}]]

tools.name: CoordinateTransform
tools.description: Converts points between coordinate systems ("Cartesian", "Polar", "Spherical", "Cylindrical", "Hyperspherical", "Elliptic", ...) with CoordinateTransform["from" -> "to", pt], CoordinateTransformData giving the transformation formulas/Jacobians and CoordinateChartData the metric, Christoffel symbols, scale factors, volume element etc. of a chart; ToPolarCoordinates/FromPolarCoordinates and ToSphericalCoordinates/FromSphericalCoordinates are the common shortcuts. Grad/Div/Curl/Laplacian (listed) accept a chart name as last argument.
tools.usage:
CoordinateTransform["Cartesian" -> "Spherical", {x, y, z}]
CoordinateTransform[{"Spherical" -> "Cartesian", 3}, {r, theta, phi}]
CoordinateTransformData["Cartesian" -> "Polar", "Mapping", {x, y}]
CoordinateChartData["Spherical", "ScaleFactors", {r, theta, phi}]
CoordinateChartData[{"Spherical", 3}, "Metric", {r, theta, phi}]
CoordinateChartData["Cylindrical", "VolumeFactor", {r, phi, z}]
Grad[f, {r, theta, phi}, "Spherical"]
ToSphericalCoordinates[{x, y, z}]

parameters.name: chart
parameters.description: Chart name, optionally with dimension {"name", n}.

tools.example:
Laplacian[f[r, theta, phi], {r, theta, phi}, "Spherical"] // Simplify
CoordinateChartData["Spherical", "Metric", {r, theta, phi}] // MatrixForm
CoordinateTransform["Cartesian" -> "Cylindrical", {1, 1, 2}]

tools.name: TransformedField
tools.description: Transforms a scalar, vector or tensor field expressed in one coordinate chart into another (e.g. a Cartesian vector field into spherical components), handling both the coordinate substitution and the basis change - the correct way to move fields between charts before applying Div/Curl in curvilinear coordinates.
tools.usage:
TransformedField["Cartesian" -> "Spherical", f, {x, y, z} -> {r, theta, phi}]
TransformedField["Cartesian" -> "Polar", {Fx, Fy}, {x, y} -> {r, phi}]
TransformedField["Cylindrical" -> "Cartesian", field, {r, phi, z} -> {x, y, z}]

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: Scalar expression, vector list or tensor in the source coordinates.

tools.example:
TransformedField["Cartesian" -> "Spherical", {x, y, z}/(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^(3/2), {x, y, z} -> {r, theta, phi}] // Simplify (* {1/r^2, 0, 0} *)
Div[%, {r, theta, phi}, "Spherical"] // Simplify (* 0 *)

tools.name: GenerateConditions
tools.description: Option of Integrate, Sum, Product, LaplaceTransform, FourierTransform, DSolve, Solve etc. controlling whether results carry validity conditions (ConditionalExpression): True always, False assumes generic parameters (fast, potentially wrong), Automatic (default) generates them when cheap; Assumptions supplies parameter assumptions (as does Assuming) and PrincipalValue -> True makes Integrate compute Cauchy principal values across singularities.
tools.usage:
Integrate[f, {x, 0, Infinity}, GenerateConditions -> False]
Integrate[f, {x, 0, Infinity}, Assumptions -> a > 0]
Integrate[1/x, {x, -1, 2}, PrincipalValue -> True]
LaplaceTransform[Exp[a t], t, s, GenerateConditions -> True]
Solve[eqns, vars, GenerateConditions -> True]
tools.example:
Integrate[Exp[-a x], {x, 0, Infinity}] (* ConditionalExpression[1/a, Re[a] > 0] *)
Integrate[Exp[-a x], {x, 0, Infinity}, Assumptions -> a > 0] (* 1/a *)
Integrate[1/(x - 1), {x, 0, 3}, PrincipalValue -> True] (* Log[2] *)

tools.name: Integrate over regions
tools.description: Integrate and NIntegrate (listed) accept region specifications - Integrate[f, {x, y} \[Element] Disk[]] or any Region (ImplicitRegion, Polygon, mesh, Boolean combinations) - and Element-based domains in Sum/Product too; with RegionMeasure, RegionCentroid and RegionMoment this makes multiple integrals over complicated domains a one-liner, and NIntegrate over MeshRegion domains integrates over FEM meshes and CAD geometry. This entry documents the region form.
tools.usage:
Integrate[f, {x, y} \[Element] Disk[{0, 0}, r]]
Integrate[f, {x, y, z} \[Element] Ball[]]
NIntegrate[f, {x, y} \[Element] ImplicitRegion[x^2 + y^4 <= 1, {x, y}]]
NIntegrate[f, {x, y, z} \[Element] mesh]
Integrate[Boole[x^2 + y^2 <= 1], {x, -1, 1}, {y, -1, 1}] (* indicator form *)
tools.example:
Integrate[x^2 + y^2, {x, y} \[Element] Disk[]] (* Pi/2 *)
NIntegrate[Exp[-x^2 - y^2], {x, y} \[Element] RegionDifference[Rectangle[{-2, -2}, {2, 2}], Disk[]]]
Integrate[1, {x, y, z} \[Element] RegionIntersection[Ball[], Cuboid[]]] (* volume: Pi/6 *)

tools.name: FunctionRange
tools.description: Finds the set of values a function takes as its variables range over the reals (or a constrained domain), returned as conditions on the output variable; the symbolic way to get exact plot ranges, bounds for optimization and images of maps.
tools.usage:
FunctionRange[f, x, y]
FunctionRange[{f, cons}, x, y]
FunctionRange[f, {x1, x2}, y]
FunctionRange[f, x, y, Complexes]
tools.example:
FunctionRange[x/(1 + x^2), x, y] (* -1/2 <= y <= 1/2 *)
FunctionRange[{Sqrt[x], 0 < x < 4}, x, y] (* 0 < y < 2 *)

tools.name: FunctionSingularities
tools.description: Finds the points (or conditions) where a function is singular - poles, branch points, essential singularities, points outside the domain of definition - over the reals or complexes; FunctionPoles restricts to poles with orders. Use it to locate where NIntegrate needs Exclusions and where series expansions fail.
tools.usage:
FunctionSingularities[f, x]
FunctionSingularities[f, x, Complexes]
FunctionSingularities[{f, cons}, x]
FunctionPoles[f, z]
FunctionPoles[f, z, "Orders"]
tools.example:
FunctionSingularities[1/(x^2 - 1) + Log[x], x] (* x == -1 || x == 0 || x == 1 *)
FunctionPoles[Gamma[z], z] (* non-positive integers *)

tools.name: FunctionConvexity
tools.description: Determines whether a function is convex (1), concave (-1) or neither (0) over the reals or a constrained domain, for one or several variables; a convex objective with convex constraints guarantees that FindMinimum/NMinimize return the global optimum and lets ConvexOptimization be used.
tools.usage:
FunctionConvexity[f, x]
FunctionConvexity[{f, cons}, {x, y}]
tools.example:
FunctionConvexity[x^2 + y^2 - x y, {x, y}] (* 1 *)
FunctionConvexity[{Log[x], x > 0}, x] (* -1: concave *)

tools.name: FunctionPeriod
tools.description: Finds the smallest period of a periodic function (or a list of periods for several variables), returning 0 for non-periodic functions; useful to set Fourier series parameters and plot ranges automatically.
tools.usage:
FunctionPeriod[f, x]
FunctionPeriod[f, {x, y}]
tools.example:
FunctionPeriod[Sin[3 x] + Cos[2 x], x] (* 2 Pi *)
FunctionPeriod[Tan[x]^2, x] (* Pi *)

tools.name: AsymptoticDSolveValue
tools.description: Gives asymptotic (series, WKB or perturbation) approximations to solutions of ordinary differential equations near a point (including regular and irregular singular points) or in a small parameter, where DSolve has no closed form; returns the truncated expansion with arbitrary constants for the general solution.
tools.usage:
AsymptoticDSolveValue[ode, y[x], {x, x0, n}]
AsymptoticDSolveValue[{ode, ics}, y[x], {x, x0, n}]
AsymptoticDSolveValue[ode, y[x], x -> Infinity]
AsymptoticDSolveValue[ode, y[x], x, {eps, 0, n}]
tools.example:
AsymptoticDSolveValue[{y''[x] + x y[x] == 0, y[0] == 1, y'[0] == 0}, y[x], {x, 0, 6}]
AsymptoticDSolveValue[y''[x] + (1 + eps x) y[x] == 0, y[x], x, {eps, 0, 1}]

tools.name: AsymptoticIntegrate
tools.description: Computes asymptotic expansions of definite (or indefinite) integrals with respect to a parameter tending to a limit - Laplace's method, stationary phase, Watson's lemma - giving leading terms when Integrate cannot evaluate the integral in closed form; AsymptoticSum and AsymptoticProduct do the same for sums and products (Euler-Maclaurin type results).
tools.usage:
AsymptoticIntegrate[f, {x, a, b}, {lambda, Infinity, n}]
AsymptoticIntegrate[f, x, {x, x0, n}]
AsymptoticSum[f, {k, 1, n}, {n, Infinity, m}]
AsymptoticProduct[f, {k, 1, n}, {n, Infinity, m}]

parameters.name: {lambda, Infinity, n}
parameters.description: Parameter, limit and number of terms.

tools.example:
AsymptoticIntegrate[Exp[-lambda x^2] Cos[x], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}, {lambda, Infinity, 2}]
AsymptoticSum[1/k, {k, 1, n}, {n, Infinity, 3}]
AsymptoticProduct[k, {k, 1, n}, {n, Infinity, 1}] (* Stirling *)

tools.name: MinLimit
tools.description: Limit inferior of a function as x approaches a point (the smallest limit of any subsequence), defined even when the ordinary Limit fails to exist; MaxLimit is the limit superior and DiscreteMinLimit the sequence version. Use them to bound oscillatory behaviour.
tools.usage:
MinLimit[f, x -> x0]
MinLimit[f, x -> Infinity]
DiscreteMinLimit[a[n], n -> Infinity]
tools.example:
MinLimit[Sin[1/x], x -> 0] (* -1 *)
MinLimit[(2 + Sin[x])/x, x -> Infinity] (* 0 *)

tools.name: ComposeSeries
tools.description: Composes two power series (substituting one SeriesData into another) to the common order, giving the expansion of f[g[x]] without recomputing from scratch; combined with InverseSeries it manipulates expansions like generating functions.
tools.usage:
ComposeSeries[s1, s2]
ComposeSeries[s1, s2, s3, ...]

parameters.name: s1, s2
parameters.description: SeriesData objects (s2 must have zero constant term for the usual composition).

tools.example: ComposeSeries[Series[Exp[x], {x, 0, 5}], Series[Sin[x], {x, 0, 5}]] (* series of Exp[Sin[x]] *)

tools.name: SumConvergence
tools.description: Tests convergence of an infinite series from its general term, returning True/False or conditions on symbolic parameters, using ratio, root, Raabe, integral and other tests (Method option); the rigorous companion of Sum for deciding whether a series result is meaningful.
tools.usage:
SumConvergence[a[k], k]
SumConvergence[a[k], k, Method -> "RatioTest"]
SumConvergence[a[k], k, Assumptions -> cond]
tools.example:
SumConvergence[1/k^p, k] (* p > 1 *)
SumConvergence[x^k/k!, k] (* True *)
SumConvergence[(-1)^k/k, k] (* True: conditionally convergent *)

tools.name: Wronskian
tools.description: Computes the Wronskian determinant of a list of functions, or of the fundamental solutions of a linear ODE given directly, to test linear independence and to apply variation of parameters; also works for systems and difference equations (Casoratian via the discrete form).
tools.usage:
Wronskian[{f1, f2, ...}, x]
Wronskian[ode, y, x]
Wronskian[{ode1, ode2}, {y1, y2}, x]
tools.example:
Wronskian[{Sin[x], Cos[x]}, x] (* -1 *)
Wronskian[y''[x] - 2 y'[x] + y[x] == 0, y, x] (* E^(2 x) up to constant *)

tools.name: MellinTransform
tools.description: Mellin transform Integral x^(s-1) f(x) dx with InverseMellinTransform, the transform adapted to scale invariance and products of functions; central to asymptotic analysis of integrals and sums, Dirichlet series and the derivation of Meijer-G representations. Returns conditions on Re[s] for convergence.
tools.usage:
MellinTransform[f, x, s]
InverseMellinTransform[F, s, x]
MellinConvolve[f, g, x, y]
tools.example:
MellinTransform[Exp[-x], x, s] (* Gamma[s] *)
MellinTransform[1/(1 + x), x, s] (* Pi Csc[Pi s], 0 < Re[s] < 1 *)

tools.name: HilbertTransform
tools.description: Symbolic Hilbert transform (principal-value convolution with 1/(Pi t)) and its inverse, which produce the quadrature component of a signal; the analytic signal f + I H[f] gives instantaneous amplitude and phase. HilbertFilter (listed) is the discrete-data version.
tools.usage:
HilbertTransform[f, t, u]
InverseHilbertTransform[F, u, t]
tools.example:
HilbertTransform[Cos[t], t, u] (* Sin[u] *)
HilbertTransform[1/(1 + t^2), t, u] (* u/(1 + u^2) *)

tools.name: FourierCosTransform
tools.description: Fourier cosine transform of a function on the half-line (even extension), with InverseFourierCosTransform; the sine version handles odd extensions. Natural for heat/diffusion problems on half-spaces with Neumann/Dirichlet boundary conditions and for real, even spectra.
tools.usage:
FourierCosTransform[f, t, w]
InverseFourierCosTransform[F, w, t]
FourierCosTransform[f, t, w, FourierParameters -> {a, b}]
tools.example:
FourierCosTransform[Exp[-t], t, w] (* Sqrt[2/Pi]/(1 + w^2) *)
FourierCosTransform[UnitBox[t/2], t, w]

tools.name: FourierCoefficient
tools.description: Gives the n-th coefficient of the complex Fourier series of a periodic function (period 2 Pi by default, adjustable with FourierParameters), while FourierSinCoefficient and FourierCosCoefficient give the trigonometric-series coefficients; the closed-form coefficients that FourierSeries/FourierTrigSeries sum.
tools.usage:
FourierCoefficient[f, t, n]
FourierCoefficient[f, t, n, FourierParameters -> {0, 2 Pi/T}]
FourierSinCoefficient[f, t, n]
FourierCosCoefficient[f, t, n]
tools.example:
FourierCoefficient[t^2, t, n] (* 2 (-1)^n/n^2 for n != 0 *)
FourierSinCoefficient[SquareWave[t/(2 Pi)], t, n] (* 4/(n Pi) for odd n *)

tools.name: SurfaceIntegrate
tools.description: Symbolic surface integral of a scalar field (weighted by area) or the flux of a vector field through a surface given as a Sphere, Cylinder, parametric or implicit region or mesh; NSurfaceIntegrate is the numerical form. Implements the divergence and Stokes theorem computations directly.
tools.usage:
SurfaceIntegrate[f, {x, y, z} \[Element] surface]
SurfaceIntegrate[{Fx, Fy, Fz}, {x, y, z} \[Element] surface]
NSurfaceIntegrate[F, {x, y, z} \[Element] surface]
tools.example:
SurfaceIntegrate[{x, y, z}, {x, y, z} \[Element] Sphere[{0, 0, 0}, R]] (* 4 Pi R^3 *)
SurfaceIntegrate[x^2, {x, y, z} \[Element] Cylinder[{{0, 0, 0}, {0, 0, 1}}, 1]]

tools.name: CoordinateChartData
tools.description: Gives properties of a coordinate chart ("Spherical", "Cylindrical", "Hyperspherical", "ProlateSpheroidal", ...): "Metric", "ScaleFactors", "ChristoffelSymbol", "VolumeFactor", "CoordinateRangeAssumptions", "OrthogonalQ", and the mapping to Cartesian coordinates - the reference data behind Grad/Div/Curl/Laplacian in curvilinear coordinates and general-relativity style tensor calculus.
tools.usage:
CoordinateChartData["chart", "prop"]
CoordinateChartData[{"chart", n}, "prop", {c1, c2, ...}]
CoordinateChartData["Spherical", "ScaleFactors", {r, theta, phi}]
CoordinateChartData["Cylindrical", "VolumeFactor", {r, phi, z}]
tools.example:
CoordinateChartData["Spherical", "Metric", {r, theta, phi}] // MatrixForm
CoordinateChartData["Spherical", "ChristoffelSymbol", {r, theta, phi}]

tools.name: DifferenceQuotient
tools.description: Gives the difference quotient (f(x+h) - f(x))/h, higher-order and partial difference quotients, the discrete analogue of D used to derive finite-difference schemes and to study discrete calculus; DifferenceDelta (listed) is the un-normalized forward difference.
tools.usage:
DifferenceQuotient[f, {x, h}]
DifferenceQuotient[f, {x, n, h}]
DifferenceQuotient[f, {x, h}, {y, k}]
tools.example:
DifferenceQuotient[x^3, {x, h}] (* 3 x^2 + 3 x h + h^2 *)
Limit[DifferenceQuotient[Sin[x], {x, h}], h -> 0] (* Cos[x] *)
